missing_spec_content.spec_text: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 × 10^-10 metres.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never gives the size of an atom. It also never uses standard form, which the spec flags as a skills point (MS 1b: 'recognise expressions given in standard form').

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of an atom.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson calls the nucleus 'tiny' but never gives its size relative to the atom.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
missing_spec_content.why: Isotopes are never defined or taught. The word appears only in tutor_note ('isotope notation'), with no explanation.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to relate differences between isotopes to differences in conventional representations of their identities, charges and masses.
missing_spec_content.why: Because isotopes are not taught, students are never shown how isotopes of one element differ in their representations.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Atoms turn into positive ions if they lose one or more outer electron(s).
missing_spec_content.why: Ion formation is not mentioned anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson starts with the plum pudding model. It never describes the earlier idea of atoms as indivisible spheres.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only says 'Bohr refined this model further (1913)'. It does not say what Bohr proposed (electrons orbiting at specific distances). It does not say that his calculations agreed with experiment.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
missing_spec_content.why: Protons are listed as particles, but how they were discovered is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
missing_spec_content.why: Neither Chadwick nor the later discovery of the neutron is mentioned.

above_gcse.text: they emit electromagnetic radiation (light) of a specific frequency. This is why each element gives a unique spectrum.
above_gcse.why: Specific frequencies and element spectra go beyond the spec. The spec only requires that electrons move to higher or lower energy levels by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation.

above_gcse.text: Bohr refined this model further (1913), and later quantum mechanics did too.
above_gcse.why: Quantum mechanics is not in the specification and could confuse the student.

above_gcse.text: The innermost shell (lowest energy) fills first, then the next, and so on.
above_gcse.why: The order in which shells fill is chemistry content. It is not in these physics spec sections.

above_gcse.text: The arrangement of outer electrons decides how atoms bond chemically.
above_gcse.why: Chemical bonding is not part of these specification sections.

above_gcse.text: Which period of the periodic table is it in?
above_gcse.why: Shell capacities and periodic table periods are chemistry content. They are not required by these physics sections.
The spec does not require relative masses of subatomic particles. The precise value 1/1836 goes beyond GCSE requirements.

factual_errors.text: (1) Most alpha particles went straight through → the atom is mostly empty space. The positive charge is not spread out as the plum pudding model said.
factual_errors.correction: The plum pudding model also predicted that most alpha particles would pass straight through, so this observation does not disprove it. The evidence that the positive charge is concentrated, not spread out, comes from the large-angle deflections and back-scattering. The lesson itself says this in keyPoints[0]: 'They would all pass straight through'.

factual_errors.text: (2) Some alpha particles were deflected at small angles → there is a small, dense, positively charged region at the centre.
factual_errors.correction: The plum pudding model predicted small deflections. The surprising evidence for a concentrated positive nucleus was that some particles were deflected through large angles. The conclusion should be tied to large-angle deflections, or simply to deflection by a positive charge.

factual_errors.text: Only direct hits cause the large deflections.
factual_errors.correction: Alpha particles do not hit the nucleus. They are strongly repelled when they come very close to it on a near head-on path.

factual_errors.text: Structure of the nucleus — protons, neutrons and electrons
factual_errors.correction: Electrons are not part of the nucleus. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, and electrons surround it.

factual_errors.text: At GCSE, you just need to know two things. Electrons are in shells at set energy levels. Moving between them emits radiation.
factual_errors.correction: Moving to a higher energy level involves absorbing electromagnetic radiation. Only moving to a lower level involves emitting it. The spec requires both.
The second shell is not filled: it holds 7 of a possible 8 electrons. It should say that two shells are occupied (in use).

wrong_terms.text: Proton number (atomic number) tells you the element.
Electrons can absorb energy to jump to a higher energy level

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.3: "An atom has 2 electrons in its first shell and 7 in its second. How many electrons does it have in total? Which period of the periodic table is it in?"
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[3].content: "Electrons can absorb energy to jump to a higher energy level... When they fall back to a lower level, they emit electromagnetic radiation"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The key point is about energy levels and absorbing or emitting radiation. The checkpoint tests electron counting and periodic table periods instead. The key point never gives shell capacities or the link between shells and periods, so the answer is not supported by it.
